h: Black swans, golden roses and a playhouse for Mary
p: Churchill bought Chartwell in 1922, and the view across the Weald was the big draw. He once said he bought it for that view, and standing on the terrace you can see why. The house opened to the public through the National Trust in 1966, and much of it is kept as it was in the 1920s and 1930s, when the family's life here was at its busiest.
Down by the lake, look out for the black swans, a nod to the birds Churchill kept on the water. Kids love spotting them, and the lakeside paths make a lovely loop.

The Golden Rose Avenue was a gift from the Churchill children to mark their parents' golden wedding anniversary in 1958, and it is a gorgeous sight when the roses are in bloom. Tucked away in the grounds is Marycot, a little brick playhouse built for Mary, the youngest Churchill daughter, which younger visitors find utterly charming.
Allow half a day to see the house, studio and gardens without rushing. The studio is a real eye-opener, with walls packed with his paintings, so give it more time than you might expect.

Nearby, Westerham is also home to Quebec House, the childhood home of General James Wolfe, now cared for by the National Trust. Emmetts Garden near Ide Hill is another lovely hillside garden close by. Head south towards Edenbridge and you will find Hever Castle, the childhood home of Anne Boleyn, which makes a fine second stop on a Kent history trip.
